# neatHack Build Brief — "Greenlight" (CI-failure → fix-PR agent)

> **For Claude Code:** Read this whole file before writing any code. It explains the hackathon, what we're building, the rules we must follow, and the build order. When something here conflicts with the official docs, the official docs win — check them and tell me.

---

## 0. TL;DR

We are building **Greenlight**: an autonomous AI agent that takes a GitHub repo with a **failing test / red CI run**, figures out why it fails, writes a fix, runs the tests, retries until they pass, and opens a **pull request** — with no human in the loop.

Every agent run is traced in **neatlogs**. The repo is built with **Entire** (checkpoints) and the agent uses **entire-graph** at runtime to understand the codebase. The business plan is made with **cfo.ai**.

**Deadline:** submission window is **Monday, Oct 12, 2026, 7:00 PM – 11:55 PM IST**. Late = not judged.

---

## 1. The hackathon in plain words

- Event: **neatHack** by neatlogs (online, 48 hours, Oct 10–12, 2026). Page: https://neatlogs.com/hackathon
- One track: **"Build an agent that works (literally)"** — an AI agent that completes a substantial task from start to finish on its own. Give it a goal, tools, and an environment; it uses each result to decide the next step.
- What judges look for in the agent: **planning, tool use, state, context, execution, recovery, verification, iteration.**

### Hard rules (do not break these)
1. **All code must be written during the hackathon** (after Oct 10, 12:30 PM IST). Do NOT copy code from any of my older projects. Commits must be dated during the event, in a **public** repo.
2. The project **must use all three**: **neatlogs**, **Entire**, **cfo.ai** — each with a clear, real role.
3. Submission = a public quote-post on X of the official neatlogs post with: team, project name, public repo, demo video link.
4. Demo video **≤ 3 minutes**, and it must explicitly cover neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai (architecture, implementation, runtime, reasoning, result for each).

### Judging weights
| Category | Weight |
|---|---|
| The agent (handles a substantial task end-to-end) | 30% |
| Use of neatlogs, Entire, cfo.ai | 25% |
| Demo video | 20% |
| Building in public (#neatHack posts) | 15% |
| Usefulness & originality | 10% |

**Implication:** 70% of the score is evidence, tool usage, demo and posting. We must deliberately produce evidence, not just code.

### Evidence judges want (we must produce ALL of these)
- [ ] **Agent improved:** a run before a change and a run after it (two neatlogs traces) with the numbers compared.
- [ ] **Used neatlogs:** trace links or screenshots.
- [ ] **Used Entire:** checkpoints (the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch) and/or entire-graph output.
- [ ] **Used cfo.ai:** business plan covering pricing, costs, revenue, runway.
- [ ] **Recovers from failures:** a run where an action failed and what the agent did next.
- [ ] **Built in public:** links to posts tagged #neatHack.
- [ ] **Code written during hackathon:** public repo, dated commits.

All evidence goes in `/evidence` and is linked from `hackathon.md` (see §9).

---

## 2. What Greenlight does (user story)

> "My CI went red. I point Greenlight at the repo. A few minutes later there's a PR with a fix, the tests are green, and the PR description explains what broke, why, and how it was verified."

### Input
- A local path or GitHub URL of a repo
- The failing test command (default: auto-detect, e.g. `npm test`) OR a failing GitHub Actions run URL/log
- A max budget: max iterations (default 5), max cost in USD (default $1)

### Output
- A git branch `greenlight/fix-<id>` with the fix
- A PR (or, in local mode, a patch file + PR-style summary)
- A run report: steps, attempts, test results, cost, tokens, neatlogs trace link

### Why this scope (and not "fix any GitHub issue")
- Input is concrete (an error log), not a vague issue description → more reliable.
- Verification is objective: tests pass or they don't.
- Failures (wrong fix, flaky test, build error) happen naturally → real recovery evidence.

---

## 3. Agent design

### 3.1 The loop

```
GOAL: make failing tests pass without breaking others

1. SETUP      clone repo → create branch → install deps
2. REPRODUCE  run test command → capture failing tests + error output
              (if nothing fails → stop: "nothing to fix")
3. LOCATE     use entire-graph to find the relevant files/symbols for the failing
              tests + stack trace (graph-first, then read only focused files)
4. PLAN       LLM writes a short plan: hypothesis of root cause + files to change
5. PATCH      LLM produces an edit (search/replace edits, not whole-file rewrites)
6. VERIFY     run the failing tests → then run the FULL suite (catch regressions)
7. DECIDE
     - all green           → go to 8
     - still failing       → feed new error + previous attempt into context,
                             update hypothesis, go to 4 (max N attempts)
     - new tests broke     → revert patch, note it, go to 4
     - tool/env error      → recovery handler (see 3.4)
     - budget exceeded     → stop, open a DRAFT PR / report with findings
8. SHIP       commit → push → open PR with summary (root cause, change, evidence)
```

### 3.2 Tools the agent can call
| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `run_command(cmd, timeout)` | run tests/builds in the repo sandbox (allow-listed commands only) |
| `graph_search(query)` | wraps `entire graph search --repo .` to locate code |
| `read_file(path, range?)` | read focused parts of files |
| `apply_edit(path, old, new)` | exact search/replace edit; fails if `old` not found exactly once |
| `revert_last_edit()` | undo the last patch |
| `git(op)` | branch, diff, commit, push |
| `open_pr(title, body)` | GitHub API (Octokit) — PR on a test repo we own |
| `finish(status, summary)` | end the run |

### 3.3 State (must survive crashes)
- Keep a `RunState` object: goal, attempt number, hypotheses tried, edits applied, test results per attempt, cost so far.
- Persist it to `runs/<run_id>/state.json` after **every step**. On restart with the same run id, **resume** from saved state instead of starting over.
- Keep context small: only send the latest error output, the current hypothesis, a short list of previously failed hypotheses, and the focused file snippets. Do NOT dump the whole repo into the prompt.

### 3.4 Recovery (this is judged — make it visible)
Handle and trace each of these explicitly:
- `apply_edit` fails (old string not found) → re-read the file, regenerate the edit.
- Test command times out → retry once with a longer timeout, then run only the failing test file.
- LLM returns malformed output / invalid tool call → re-prompt with the validation error (max 2).
- Patch causes new failures → revert and record the hypothesis as "rejected".
- API rate limit / network error → exponential backoff.
- Out of attempts/budget → stop gracefully with a draft PR/report explaining what was tried.

Each recovery must appear as a visible span/event in neatlogs (e.g. tag `recovery:<type>`).

### 3.5 Verification
- A fix is only "done" if: originally failing tests now pass **AND** the full suite has no new failures **AND** the diff doesn't delete or skip tests (check the diff for `.skip`, `xit`, deleted test files, etc. — reject such "fixes").

---

## 4. Tech stack

- **Language:** TypeScript, Node.js 20+
- **Agent loop:** hand-written loop using the **Anthropic SDK** (`@anthropic-ai/sdk`) with tool use. (Alternative if it's faster: Vercel AI SDK. neatlogs documents integrations for Anthropic, Vercel AI SDK, Claude Agent SDK, Mastra — **check https://docs.neatlogs.com/integrations and pick whichever has the cleanest TS tracing**.)
- **Model:** a Claude model via Anthropic API (or Amazon Bedrock if we get AWS credits).
- **Tracing:** neatlogs TypeScript SDK — https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/typescript
- **Code graph:** entire-graph CLI (called via child process)
- **GitHub:** Octokit (`@octokit/rest`) with a fine-grained token scoped ONLY to our test repos
- **CLI:** `commander` or plain `process.argv`
- **Optional UI:** none for v1. A tiny web page showing live run status only if time permits (stretch).

### Project structure (proposal)
```
greenlight/
├── src/
│   ├── index.ts            # CLI entry: greenlight run --repo <path> [--test "npm test"]
│   ├── agent/loop.ts       # the plan → patch → verify → decide loop
│   ├── agent/prompts.ts    # system + step prompts
│   ├── agent/state.ts      # RunState + persist/resume
│   ├── tools/              # run_command, graph_search, files, git, github
│   ├── recovery.ts         # recovery handlers
│   ├── verify.ts           # test-result parsing + "no cheating" diff checks
│   └── tracing.ts          # neatlogs init, span helpers, tags, flush/shutdown
├── bench/
│   ├── repos/              # seeded buggy test repos (see §6)
│   └── run-bench.ts        # runs agent on all cases, outputs results table
├── evidence/               # screenshots, trace links, before/after tables
├── runs/                   # run state (gitignored)
├── hackathon.md            # build log (see §9)
├── README.md
└── .env.example
```

---

## 5. Sponsor tool integration (the 25%)

### 5.1 neatlogs — tracing + improvement loop
**Setup (verify exact commands in docs):**
- Get API key at https://app.neatlogs.com
- Install the official agent skill so you (Claude Code) instrument correctly: `npx skills add neatlogs/skills` (see https://docs.neatlogs.com/integrations/skills — pick the TypeScript skill if one exists)
- Connect the neatlogs **MCP server** to Claude Code: `npx @neatlogs/wizard mcp --api-key <KEY>` (or add to `.mcp.json`: type `http`, url `https://ingest.neatlogs.com/mcp`, header `Authorization: Bearer <KEY>`).

**What to trace:**
- One trace per agent run; workflow name `greenlight`.
- Spans: `agent` (whole run) → `llm` (plan/patch calls) → `tool` (each tool call) → custom spans for `verify` and `recovery`.
- Tags/attributes: `run_id`, `bench_case`, `attempt`, `agent_version` (v1/v2…), `outcome` (fixed / gave_up / regressed), `recovery:<type>`.
- Use sessions to group all runs of one benchmark pass.
- Always `flush()`/`shutdown()` at the end of a run so traces aren't lost.
- Redact secrets/tokens (see PII redaction docs).

**How we USE it (this is the story for judges):**
1. Run benchmark with agent **v1** → collect traces.
2. In Claude Code, use the neatlogs MCP (`search_traces`, `get_trace_context`, `triage_list`) to find why runs failed.
3. Fix the agent → **v2** → rerun benchmark.
4. Record the comparison: success rate, avg attempts, avg tokens, avg cost, avg latency. Save to `evidence/before-after.md` with trace links.

### 5.2 Entire — build-time AND runtime
**Build time (proves how we built it):**
- Install CLI: `curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash`
- In repo: `entire enable --agent claude-code`
- Checkpoints are created on each commit and stored on branch `entire/checkpoints/v1`. **Make sure this branch is pushed** to the public repo. Commit often with clear messages.

**Runtime (the agent itself uses Entire):**
- Install entire-graph (see https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph — Go install + `entire plugin install`).
- Agent indexes the target repo: `entire graph index --repo .`
- `graph_search` tool wraps `entire graph search --repo .` so the agent locates code from a graph instead of grep-and-read.
- Trace graph calls in neatlogs and log "graph-first" stats (how many locate steps used the graph).
- Save sample graph output to `evidence/entire-graph-sample.txt`.

### 5.3 cfo.ai — business plan (done by me, the human; you help with numbers)
- Signup: https://cfo.ai/neathacks (card required — cancel immediately in Settings → Billing; credits come from the neatHack team).
- **Your job:** produce `evidence/unit-economics.md` from REAL neatlogs data: avg cost per run, avg cost per successful fix, success rate, avg time to fix.
- I will feed those numbers to cfo.ai and model: pricing (e.g. per fixed CI failure, or monthly per repo), infra + inference costs, revenue scenarios, runway. Export goes in `evidence/cfo-business-plan.pdf` (or screenshots).
- Comparison to include: cost per automated fix vs. engineer time to fix a red build.

---

## 6. The benchmark (build this FIRST — everything depends on it)

Create a small set of seeded buggy repos we own, so demos are reliable and we can measure improvement.

- Make **1–2 small TypeScript/JS projects** (e.g. a utility library + a tiny Express API) with a real test suite (Vitest or Jest).
- Create **~10 cases**, each = one git branch or patch that introduces a bug making specific tests fail. Mix difficulty:
  - easy: off-by-one, wrong operator, typo in a key
  - medium: bug in a different file than the failing test, wrong async/await
  - hard: two-file fix, a fix where the "obvious" patch breaks another test (forces regression handling)
  - 1 flaky/timeout case (forces recovery)
- `bench/run-bench.ts` runs the agent on every case and writes a results table: case, outcome, attempts, tokens, cost, time, trace link.
- Also push one case to a GitHub repo with Actions so we can demo the real "red CI → PR" flow end to end.

---

## 7. Build order / milestones

Times are IST. Commit and push after every milestone. Post a #neatHack update at each ⭐.

**M0 — Setup (first ~1–2 hrs)**
- Repo created (public), Entire enabled, neatlogs key + MCP connected, `.env.example`, README stub, `hackathon.md` started. ⭐

**M1 — Benchmark repos (~2–3 hrs)**
- Seeded buggy projects + 10 cases + verify each case actually fails.

**M2 — Agent v1 end-to-end (Day 1 evening)**
- Loop works on 1 easy case locally: reproduce → locate → patch → verify → commit. Traced in neatlogs. ⭐

**M3 — Tools + recovery + state (Day 1 night)**
- entire-graph tool, revert, retries, persist/resume, anti-cheat diff check.

**M4 — Benchmark v1 (Day 2 morning)**
- Run all 10 cases → save results table + traces as the "before". ⭐

**M5 — Improve → v2 (Day 2)**
- Diagnose failures using neatlogs MCP, fix prompts/tools/context, rerun → "after" table. ⭐

**M6 — Real GitHub flow (Day 2 evening)**
- Red Actions run → Greenlight → PR opened with good description. ⭐

**M7 — Business + evidence (Day 3 morning)**
- unit-economics.md, cfo.ai plan, evidence folder complete, README polished.

**M8 — Demo + submit (Day 3, done by ~6 PM)**
- Record ≤3 min video, final README, submit on X at 7 PM when window opens. ⭐

**If time runs short, cut in this order:** web UI → GitHub Actions trigger (keep local mode) → hard bench cases. **Never cut:** neatlogs before/after, recovery evidence, Entire checkpoints, cfo.ai plan.

---

## 8. Demo video plan (≤ 3:00)

1. **0:00–0:20** Problem: red CI wastes engineer time. Greenlight fixes it autonomously.
2. **0:20–1:10** Live run: red build → agent reproduces, searches graph, patches, a test fails, it recovers, tests go green, PR opens.
3. **1:10–1:45** **neatlogs:** trace span tree of that run; a failed run; MCP used to diagnose; v1 vs v2 numbers.
4. **1:45–2:15** **Entire:** checkpoints branch showing how we built it + entire-graph used at runtime by the agent.
5. **2:15–2:45** **cfo.ai:** pricing, cost per fix (from neatlogs data), revenue scenarios, runway.
6. **2:45–3:00** Results recap + repo link.

---

## 9. hackathon.md (keep updated after every work session)

Sections:
- **Project:** name, one-sentence purpose, problem
- **Team:** (I'll fill in)
- **Stack:** actual services used
- **Build log:** dated entries — what changed, experiments, failures, fixes, evidence links. Separate *planned* from *done*.
- **Demo:** how to run + video link
- **Known limitations & next steps**
- **Submission checklist:** the evidence list from §1, ticked off

Optional helper: neatlogs publishes a hackathon skill at https://neatlogs.com/hackathon/skill that maintains this log.

---

## 10. Guardrails for you (Claude Code)

- **Never commit secrets.** `.env` is gitignored; use `.env.example`. Double-check before every push.
- **Never fabricate** benchmark results, trace links, or numbers. If something didn't run, say so.
- The agent may only run allow-listed commands, only inside the target repo directory, and only push/open PRs on repos we own.
- Small, frequent commits with clear messages (Entire checkpoints depend on commits).
- If an API/command in this brief doesn't match the official docs, **check the docs, follow them, and tell me what changed**.
- Ask me before: choosing a different scope, adding paid services, or anything that posts publicly.

---

## 11. Useful links

- Hackathon: https://neatlogs.com/hackathon
- neatlogs docs: https://docs.neatlogs.com · TS SDK: https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/typescript · MCP: https://docs.neatlogs.com/integrations/mcp
- neatlogs GitHub: https://github.com/NeatLogs/neatlogs · Skills: https://github.com/neatlogs/skills

- cfo.ai signup: https://cfo.ai/neathacks · docs: https://docs.cfo.ai
- Crustdata API (optional): https://www.crustdata.com/api-documentation

## 12. First thing to do right now

1. Confirm you've read this brief and summarize the plan back in 5 lines.
2. Do **M0** (setup). Stop and show me before starting M1. let's get started

# Entire CLI: Installation & Setup Guide

## Installation

Choose your platform:

**macOS/Linux (Homebrew):**
```bash
brew install --cask entireio/tap/entire
```

**macOS/Linux (Script):**
```bash
curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash
```

**Windows (PowerShell):**
```powershell
irm https://entire.io/install.ps1 | iex
```

**Go (Development):**
```bash
go install github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire@latest
go install github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/git-remote-entire@latest
```

## Enable in Your Repository

```bash
cd your-project
entire enable --agent claude-code
entire status
```

Replace `claude-code` with: `cursor`, `codex`, `antigravity`, `pi`, `copilot-cli`, `opencode`, or `factoryai-droid`.

## How Checkpoints Work

Checkpoints are stored as independent Git references at `refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>`. The system captures your AI session data separately from your commit history—when you commit, Entire creates a checkpoint snapshot linked via an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer in your commit message.

Key distinction: "Your commits stay clean; session metadata lives in per-checkpoint refs."

## Requirements Before Use

**Authentication:** Run `entire login` (opens browser by default). For headless environments, use `--device` flag or set `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file`.

**Account:** Requires an Entire account; no explicit signup mentioned—authentication establishes access.

**Git & OS:** Git required; works on macOS, Linux, or Windows.

**Supported Agent:** Must have one installed and authenticated (Claude Code, Cursor, etc.).

# Entire Graph Installation and Usage

## Installation

Entire Graph requires Entire CLI 0.10.0+ and Git 2.36+. Install the CLI first:

**macOS/Linux:**
```bash
curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash
```

Then install the plugin:
```bash
entire plugin install graph
entire graph version
```

## Indexing a Repository

To prepare a repo for agent use:
```bash
entire graph init-agents --repo .
```

This creates configuration files in `.entire/` and updates `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md`.

For prewarming the index cache:
```bash
entire graph index
```

## Command-Line Search Syntax

**Basic query:**
```bash
entire graph query "plain language description"
```

**Query with options:**
```bash
entire graph query --profile full "search terms"
entire graph query --head "search terms"  # committed tree only
```

**Other key commands:**
```bash
entire graph def <symbol>           # lookup definition
entire graph neighbors <symbol>     # trace callers/callees
entire graph impact --symbol <name> # blast radius analysis
entire graph diff                   # semantic changes between revisions
```

## Output Format

Query results return JSON containing:
- Ranked matches with source snippets
- File and line locations (`file:line` format)
- Context budgets and ranking explanations

The documentation notes that "ranked code search from plain-language task descriptions" combines lexical and graph-based matching, with results prioritized by relevance to the query.

For prewarming the index cache:
```bash
entire graph index
```

## Command-Line Search Syntax

**Basic query:**
```bash
entire graph query "plain language description"
```

**Query with options:**
```bash
entire graph query --profile full "search terms"
entire graph query --head "search terms"  # committed tree only
```

**Other key commands:**
```bash
entire graph def <symbol>           # lookup definition
entire graph neighbors <symbol>     # trace callers/callees
entire graph impact --symbol <name> # blast radius analysis
entire graph diff                   # semantic changes between revisions
```

## Output Format

Query results return JSON containing:
- Ranked matches with source snippets
- File and line locations (`file:line` format)
- Context budgets and ranking explanations

The documentation notes that "ranked code search from plain-language task descriptions" combines lexical and graph-based matching, with results prioritized by relevance to the query.

# Greenlight

> An autonomous agent that takes a repo with a failing test suite / red CI run, figures out why, writes a fix, verifies it, and opens a pull request — no human in the loop.

Built for [neatHack](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon) (Oct 10–12, 2026).

## Status

🚧 Under active development during the hackathon. See [`hackathon.md`](./hackathon.md) for the build log and evidence checklist.

## What it does

1. Point Greenlight at a repo with a failing test command (or a red GitHub Actions run).
2. It reproduces the failure, locates the relevant code via [Entire](https://entire.io)'s code graph, forms a hypothesis, and patches it.
3. It verifies: originally-failing tests pass, the full suite has no new failures, and no tests were deleted/skipped to "cheat" the fix.
4. If verification fails, it retries with a new hypothesis (up to a budget), recovering from tool errors, timeouts, and regressions along the way.
5. On success, it opens a PR with a summary of the root cause, the fix, and the evidence.

Every run is traced end-to-end in [neatlogs](https://neatlogs.com).

## Stack

- TypeScript / Node.js 20+
- Anthropic SDK (agent loop + tool use), traced via the neatlogs TypeScript SDK
- [Entire](https://entire.io) for build checkpoints and the `entire-graph` runtime code graph
- [cfo.ai](https://cfo.ai) for the business plan (see `evidence/`)

## Quickstart

```bash
npm install
cp .env.example .env   # fill in ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, NEATLOGS_API_KEY, GITHUB_TOKEN
npm run dev -- run --repo <path-to-repo> --test "npm test"
```

## Project layout

```
src/        agent loop, tools, tracing, recovery, verification
bench/      seeded buggy repos + benchmark runner
evidence/   traces, before/after numbers, business plan, screenshots
hackathon.md  dated build log + submission evidence checklist
```

## Evidence

See [`hackathon.md`](./hackathon.md) for links to traces, benchmark results, and the business plan.

input.prompt:
Execute M1 from the Greenlight build brief: seed the benchmark repos and 10 bug cases. Work in /Users/vedmohan/Projects/something (the greenlight repo, already git-initialized, already has an M0 commit pushed to https://github.com/ivedmohan/greenlight on branch main, Entire is enabled and logged in, neatlogs key is in .env).

GOAL: produce `bench/repos/` (golden, all-tests-passing seed projects) and `bench/cases/` (one patch + metadata per bug case), such that applying a case's patch to the golden repo makes specific tests fail — verified by actually running the tests, not assumed.

## Two seed projects

### 1. `bench/repos/stringkit/` — small TS utility library
Use vitest. package.json with "test": "vitest run", devDependencies vitest + typescript, dependencies none. tsconfig minimal (ES2022, NodeNext or CommonJS — your call, keep it simple and working).

Files:
- `src/internal/normalize.ts` — exports `normalizeForSlug(s: string): string` (lowercase, trim, replace non-alphanumeric runs with `-`, strip leading/trailing `-`) and `isPlainObject(v: unknown): boolean` (true only for plain objects, false for arrays/null/primitives — this matters, see hard-1 case below).
- `src/capitalize.ts` — `capitalize(s: string): string` → uppercase first char + rest unchanged.
- `src/slugify.ts` — `slugify(s: string): string`, uses `normalizeForSlug` from internal/normalize.ts.
- `src/truncate.ts` — `truncate(s: string, maxLen: number): string`, appends "..." if truncated.
- `src/numbers.ts` — `sum(nums: number[]): number` and `clamp(n: number, min: number, max: number): number`.
- `src/arrays.ts` — `chunk<T>(arr: T[], size: number): T[][]`, `unique<T>(arr: T[]): T[]`, `flattenDeep(arr: any[]): any[]`.
- `src/compare.ts` — `deepEqual(a: unknown, b: unknown): boolean`, uses `isPlainObject` from internal/normalize.ts for recursive object comparison (and handles arrays separately, correctly, in the golden version).
- `src/merge.ts` — `merge(a: object, b: object): object` shallow merge, uses `isPlainObject` from internal/normalize.ts to validate both inputs are plain objects (throws if not).
- `src/retry.ts` — `async function retryWithBackoff<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>, attempts: number, baseDelayMs: number): Promise<T>` — retries fn, delay = baseDelayMs * 2^attemptIndex, rethrows last error after attempts exhausted.
- `src/index.ts` — barrel re-exporting everything above.

Test files (one per concern), real assertions, each test file must be meaningful (3-6 test cases):
- `test/capitalize.test.ts`
- `test/slugify.test.ts`
- `test/truncate.test.ts`
- `test/numbers.test.ts` (sum + clamp)
- `test/arrays.test.ts` (chunk + unique + flattenDeep)
- `test/compare.test.ts` (deepEqual — include a case comparing an array vs a plain object with matching numeric keys, which must be `false`)
- `test/merge.test.ts` (merge — include a case asserting `merge([1,2], {a:1})` throws, i.e. arrays are rejected as non-plain-objects)
- `test/retry.test.ts` (retryWithBackoff — assert it eventually resolves after N failures, assert it rejects after exhausting attempts, assert total elapsed time for 2 retries with small baseDelayMs is well under a loose upper bound e.g. < 2000ms for baseDelayMs=10)

Run `npm install && npm test` in this dir and confirm ALL tests pass before proceeding. Fix bugs in your own golden code if they don't.

### 2. `bench/repos/tasks-api/` — tiny Express API
package.json: express + devDependencies vitest + supertest + @types/express + @types/supertest + typescript. "test": "vitest run".

Files:
- `src/store.ts` — in-memory array, `listTasks(filter?: {completed?: boolean}): Task[]`, `createTask(input): Task`, `updateTask(id, patch): Task | undefined`, `deleteTask(id): boolean`. Task = {id: string, title: string, completed: boolean}.
- `src/validate.ts` — `validateTask(input: {title?: unknown; completed?: unknown}, opts: {partial: boolean}): {valid: boolean; errors: string[]}`. Rules: title required (non-empty after trim) UNLESS opts.partial is true AND title is undefined (partial update may omit title, but if present it must still be non-empty after trim and <= 100 chars). completed, if present, must be boolean.
- `src/routes.ts` — Express Router: GET /tasks (supports ?completed=true/false query filter), POST /tasks (validate with partial:false), PATCH /tasks/:id (validate with partial:true, 404 if id not found), DELETE /tasks/:id (404 if not found).
- `src/app.ts` — builds and exports the Express app (json middleware + routes mounted at /tasks), no `listen()` call here.
- `src/index.ts` — imports app, calls `app.listen(...)` (not exercised by tests).

Test file `test/tasks.test.ts` using supertest against the app from `src/app.ts` (import app directly, no real server needed). Cover: list empty, create valid, create rejects empty/whitespace title, create rejects title > 100 chars, list filters by ?completed=true and ?completed=false correctly, update (partial, title omitted) succeeds and keeps other fields, update with empty-string title is rejected, delete removes it and then GET /tasks/:id-equivalent (list) no longer includes it, update/delete on unknown id returns 404.

IMPORTANT: reset the in-memory store between tests (e.g. an exported `resetStore()` from store.ts called in a `beforeEach`), so tests are independent.

Run `npm install && npm test` in this dir and confirm ALL tests pass before proceeding.

## The 10 bug cases

For EACH case: take the golden project, introduce exactly the bug described, run the test suite, CONFIRM the actual failing tests match what's expected (if they don't, adjust the bug until they do — do not fabricate), then produce a unified diff patch (`diff -u` recursively over the changed file(s), or `git diff --no-index <golden-file> <buggy-file>` per file) and revert the working copy back to golden state. Store outputs under `bench/cases/<project>/<case-id>/`:
  - `bug.patch` — unified diff(s) that convert golden -> buggy (paths inside the patch should be relative to the project root, e.g. `src/capitalize.ts`, so it can be applied with `patch -p0` or `patch -p1` from the project root — pick one convention and document it in `bench/README.md`)
  - `meta.json` — `{"id", "project", "difficulty": "easy"|"medium"|"hard"|"flaky", "description", "expected_failing_tests": [...test file names or test names...], "expected_passing_tests_still_pass": true}`

Cases (project: stringkit unless noted):
1. `easy-capitalize` — bug: `capitalize` duplicates the first char or drops a char (e.g. uses `s.slice(0)` instead of `s.slice(1)` when concatenating). Only `test/capitalize.test.ts` fails.
2. `easy-clamp` — bug: wrong order/operator in `clamp` (e.g. swaps min/max application or uses `<` where `<=` needed) so boundary values are wrong. Only the clamp assertions in `test/numbers.test.ts` fail (sum assertions still pass).
3. `easy-sum` — bug: `sum` reduce starts at a non-zero initial value (e.g. 1 instead of 0). Only the sum assertions in `test/numbers.test.ts` fail.
4. `medium-slugify-shared-helper` — bug is in `src/internal/normalize.ts`'s `normalizeForSlug` (e.g. a regex that also strips digits), NOT in `src/slugify.ts`. Only `test/slugify.test.ts` fails — this is the "fix is in a different file than the obviously-related one" case.
5. `medium-retry-missing-await` — bug: `retryWithBackoff` fails to `await` the call to `fn()` inside its try block, so a synchronously-thrown error isn't caught correctly OR a rejected promise isn't caught (pick whichever is more realistic to implement and actually breaks a test). Only `test/retry.test.ts` fails.
6. `hard-shared-isPlainObject` — bug is in `isPlainObject` in `src/internal/normalize.ts` (e.g. it returns true for arrays too, by just checking `typeof v === 'object' && v !== null` without excluding `Array.isArray`). This must break BOTH `test/compare.test.ts` (the array-vs-object-with-numeric-keys deepEqual case) AND `test/merge.test.ts` (the "merge rejects arrays" case). A fix must correctly exclude arrays in `isPlainObject` itself — confirm that fixing it there (not patching each call site separately) makes both test files pass.
7. `flaky-retry-backoff-explosion` — bug: the backoff formula in `retryWithBackoff` uses `baseDelayMs ** (attemptIndex + 2)` or similar so delays balloon to multi-second/minute scale even for small baseDelayMs used in the test, causing `test/retry.test.ts`'s elapsed-time assertion to fail AND/or the test to hang past a normal timeout. Confirm with a wall-clock timed test run that this is measurably slow/timing out, not just a value mismatch.
8. `medium-tasks-update-store-bug` (project: tasks-api) — bug in `src/store.ts`'s `updateTask` (e.g. it returns a stale copy, or mutates a different object, or fails to persist the patch into the stored array) so the PATCH route in `routes.ts` (which is correct) returns wrong/stale data. Only the update-related tests in `test/tasks.test.ts` fail.
9. `hard-tasks-validate-partial-flag-ignored` (project: tasks-api) — bug in `src/validate.ts`: the `opts.partial` flag is ignored for the "title required" check, so PATCH requests that omit `title` are wrongly rejected as invalid. This must break the "update (partial, title omitted) succeeds" test. A correct fix must still keep title required on CREATE (partial:false) — confirm a fix that just removes the required-check entirely would break the "create rejects empty title" test (note this in meta.json's description so we know it's a real hard case), but your actual bug+expected-failing-tests should reflect ONLY the partial-update test failing when the bug is applied naively as described.
10. `easy-tasks-completed-filter` (project: tasks-api) — bug in `src/store.ts`'s `listTasks` filter: compares `t.completed === filter.completed` where `filter.completed` arrives as a string from the query parser instead of being coerced to boolean in `routes.ts` (i.e. the bug is routes.ts not converting `req.query.completed` to a real boolean before passing to store). Only the completed-filter test(s) in `test/tasks.test.ts` fail.

## bench/run-bench.ts (minimal version for M1 — just verification, not the agent yet)

Write a TypeScript script (run via `tsx bench/run-bench.ts`) that, for every case in `bench/cases/**/meta.json`:
1. Copies the case's golden project (`bench/repos/<project>`) to a temp dir under `runs/bench-verify/<case-id>/` (gitignored — runs/ is already gitignored).
2. Copies/symlinks `node_modules` from the golden project into the temp copy (don't re-run npm install for every case — too slow; just reuse the golden project's installed node_modules, e.g. copy the directory or create a symlink).
3. Applies `bug.patch` (document and use whichever of `patch -p0`/`-p1`/`git apply` you actually used when generating patches — be consistent).
4. Runs the test command, captures pass/fail per test file.
5. Prints a results table (case id, difficulty, expected vs actual failing tests, PASS/FAIL on "matches expectation").
6. Exit code 0 only if every case's actual failure matches its `meta.json` expectation.

Run `tsx bench/run-bench.ts` (install `tsx` as a root devDependency if not already present — it should already be in the root package.json from M0) and confirm it reports all 10 cases matching expectations. Fix cases that don't match (adjust the bug or the expectation, based on the REAL observed output — never fabricate a passing result).

## Also write `bench/README.md`

Explain: the two seed projects, the patch format/apply convention, how to add a new case, and how to run `bench/run-bench.ts`.

## Finish

- Update `/Users/vedmohan/Projects/something/hackathon.md`: add a new dated entry (use today's actual date, check with `date`) under "Build log" for M1, summarizing what was built, the 10 cases (one line each: id, difficulty, one-line description), and noting the verification run passed all 10 (or listing any that don't, honestly, if you ran out of time to fix them — DO NOT claim success you didn't verify). Also tick the "Code written during hackathon" box is still true, leave other checklist items unchecked (they're not done yet).
- Stage and commit everything (`bench/`, updated `hackathon.md`) with git, in reasonably small logical commits if it makes sense (e.g. one commit for stringkit, one for tasks-api, one for cases+runner+README+hackathon.md update) or one clean commit if that's simpler — your judgment. Use the commit trailer `Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>` on every commit.
- Push to `origin main`.
- `runs/` must stay gitignored — do not commit anything under `runs/`.

## Constraints
- Do not touch `src/`, `src/tracing.ts`, `src/index.ts`, or anything else from M0 at the repo root — this is purely additive under `bench/` plus the hackathon.md update.
- Do not install or configure neatlogs/Entire/cfo.ai in this task — that's other milestones.
- Never fabricate test results, patch contents, or the verification table. If something doesn't work after reasonable effort, report exactly what's broken instead of claiming it works.
- Keep network/package installs to just `npm install` in the two bench/repos projects (and tsx at root if missing) — nothing exotic.

## Report back
When done, report concisely (under 300 words): what was created, the verification table result (all 10 matching or not), what was committed/pushed (commit hashes/messages), and any deviations from this spec you had to make and why.

input.content:
# Bench

Seeded buggy repos used to measure Greenlight's reliability with real before/after numbers instead of vibes.

## Layout

```
bench/
├── repos/<project>/        golden, all-tests-passing seed project
├── cases/<project>/<id>/   one bug case:
│     bug.patch               unified diff, golden -> buggy
│     meta.json               difficulty, description, expected failing tests
└── run-bench.ts            verifies every case's patch actually produces the expected failures
```

## Seed projects

- **`stringkit`** — a small TS utility library (capitalize, slugify, truncate, sum/clamp, array helpers, deepEqual, merge, retryWithBackoff). 8 test files, 36 tests, all passing on `main`.
- **`tasks-api`** — a tiny Express CRUD API for tasks, tested with supertest against the app directly (no real server/port). 1 test file, 13 tests, all passing on `main`.

## Patch format

Patches are generated with `diff -u <golden-file> <buggy-file>`, with the diff header paths rewritten to be relative to the project root (e.g. `src/capitalize.ts`). Apply them with:

```bash
cd bench/repos/<project>   # or a copy of it
patch -p0 < ../../cases/<project>/<case-id>/bug.patch
```

`-p0` (not `-p1`) because the paths in the patch are already project-root-relative with no extra leading directory component.

## The 10 cases

| id | project | difficulty | what's wrong |
|---|---|---|---|
| `easy-capitalize` | stringkit | easy | `capitalize()` duplicates the first char instead of dropping it (`slice(0)` vs `slice(1)`) |
| `easy-clamp` | stringkit | easy | `clamp()` off-by-one at the max boundary |
| `easy-sum` | stringkit | easy | `sum()` reduce starts at 1 instead of 0 |
| `medium-slugify-shared-helper` | stringkit | medium | bug lives in `internal/normalize.ts`, not in `slugify.ts` — the file most obviously related to the failing test is NOT where the fix goes |
| `medium-retry-missing-await` | stringkit | medium | missing `await` on an inner async call breaks error handling |
| `hard-shared-isplainobject` | stringkit | hard | one shared helper (`isPlainObject`) bug breaks two unrelated test files (`compare.test.ts` and `merge.test.ts`) at once; the fix must go in the shared helper, not one call site |
| `flaky-retry-backoff-explosion` | stringkit | flaky | backoff formula explodes, causing genuine test **timeouts**, not just wrong assertions — exercises the agent's timeout-recovery path |
| `easy-completed-filter` | tasks-api | easy | query-string boolean isn't coerced before being passed to the store's filter |
| `medium-update-store-bug` | tasks-api | medium | `updateTask()` returns a non-persisted copy; the route code calling it is correct — cross-file root cause |
| `hard-validate-partial-flag-ignored` | tasks-api | hard | shared validation function ignores the `partial` flag for the required-title check, breaking PATCH while CREATE still needs to require a title — the fix must be conditional, not a blanket removal |

## Adding a new case

1. Copy the golden project to a scratch dir (outside `bench/`, e.g. under `runs/`, which is gitignored).
2. Introduce the bug, run the project's tests, and read the actual output — don't guess which tests fail.
3. `diff -u bench/repos/<project>/<file> <scratch>/<file> | sed 's|bench/repos/<project>/||; s|<scratch>/||' > bench/cases/<project>/<id>/bug.patch`
4. Write `meta.json` with the **observed** failing test names, not the intended ones.
5. Revert the scratch copy, then run `tsx bench/run-bench.ts` and confirm the new case passes.

## Running the verification

```bash
npx tsx bench/run-bench.ts
```

For each case this copies the golden project to `runs/bench-verify/<project>/<id>/` (symlinking in `node_modules` from the golden project so it doesn't reinstall for every case), applies the patch, runs the test suite, and checks the observed failing test files against `meta.json`. Exits non-zero if any case doesn't match.

# Greenlight — neatHack build log

## Project

**Name:** Greenlight
**One-sentence purpose:** An autonomous agent that turns a red CI run into a merged-ready pull request, with no human in the loop.
**Problem:** Engineers lose time triaging and fixing routine test failures; Greenlight handles the reproduce → locate → patch → verify → recover loop end to end.

## Team

- zoro (solo, so far)

## Stack

- TypeScript / Node.js 20+, Anthropic SDK
- neatlogs (tracing) — TS SDK
- Entire (build checkpoints) + entire-graph (runtime code graph)
- cfo.ai (business plan)
- GitHub Actions + Octokit (real red-CI → PR demo)

## Build log

### 2026-10-11 — M0: Setup
- Repo initialized, public GitHub repo created under `ivedmohan`.
- Entire CLI 0.11.4 installed via Homebrew; `entire enable` + `entire login` pending (human step).
- Neatlogs API key wired into `.env` (gitignored); project ID `73ddd324-c4e6-48fd-8667-2db6335ae52d`.
- Project scaffolded: `src/` (agent, tools, tracing), `bench/`, `evidence/`.
- Noted doc discrepancies vs. the original build brief:
  - Entire checkpoints are git refs at `refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>` (linked via `Entire-Checkpoint` commit trailer), not a `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch.
  - entire-graph's search command is `entire graph query "<text>"`, not `entire graph search`. Setup is `entire graph init-agents --repo .` then `entire graph index`.

**Planned next:** M1 — seed the benchmark repos (10 buggy cases).

## Demo

_TBD — added at M8._

## Known limitations & next steps

_TBD._

## Submission checklist

- [ ] Agent improved: before/after neatlogs traces compared
- [ ] Used neatlogs: trace links / screenshots
- [ ] Used Entire: checkpoint refs + entire-graph output
- [ ] Used cfo.ai: business plan (pricing, costs, revenue, runway)
- [ ] Recovers from failures: a traced run showing a failure + recovery
- [ ] Built in public: #neatHack post links
- [ ] Code written during hackathon: dated commits in a public repo

- `entire login` completed (human step); `entire auth status` confirms logged in as `github:ivedmohan`, checkpoints syncing to `origin`.

### 2026-10-11 — M1: Benchmark repos
- Built two golden seed projects under `bench/repos/`:
  - `stringkit` — TS utility library (capitalize, slugify, truncate, sum/clamp, array helpers, deepEqual, merge, retryWithBackoff). 8 test files, 36/36 tests passing.
  - `tasks-api` — tiny Express CRUD API for tasks, tested with supertest. 1 test file, 13/13 tests passing.
- Seeded 10 bug cases under `bench/cases/<project>/<id>/` (a `bug.patch` unified diff + `meta.json` with the difficulty and the *observed*, not assumed, failing tests):
  - `easy-capitalize` (stringkit) — `slice(0)` vs `slice(1)` duplicates the first char.
  - `easy-clamp` (stringkit) — off-by-one at the max boundary.
  - `easy-sum` (stringkit) — reduce starts at 1 instead of 0.
  - `medium-slugify-shared-helper` (stringkit) — bug is in `internal/normalize.ts`, not `slugify.ts`.
  - `medium-retry-missing-await` (stringkit) — missing `await` breaks error handling in `retryWithBackoff`.
  - `hard-shared-isplainobject` (stringkit) — one shared-helper bug breaks two unrelated test files at once (`compare.test.ts` + `merge.test.ts`); fix must go in the shared helper.
  - `flaky-retry-backoff-explosion` (stringkit) — backoff formula explodes, causing genuine test **timeouts** (verified at `--testTimeout=3000`, all 3 tests time out), not just wrong assertions.
  - `easy-completed-filter` (tasks-api) — query-string boolean not coerced before filtering.
  - `medium-update-store-bug` (tasks-api) — `updateTask()` returns a non-persisted copy; route code is correct, bug is cross-file.
  - `hard-validate-partial-flag-ignored` (tasks-api) — shared validation ignores the `partial` flag, breaking PATCH while CREATE still needs the required-title check; fix must be conditional.
- Wrote `bench/run-bench.ts`: for every case, copies the golden project, applies its patch, runs the real test suite, and checks observed failing test files against `meta.json`. **Ran it: 10/10 cases match their expectation** (verified, not assumed — see terminal output captured during the build session).
- Wrote `bench/README.md` documenting the layout, patch format/apply convention (`patch -p0`), and how to add a case.
- Noted deviation from the original case list in the build brief: case descriptions/exact bugs were adjusted from the initial plan where the first attempt didn't reproduce the intended failure (e.g. `compare.ts`'s array-handling had to be simplified so the `hard-shared-isplainobject` bug could actually manifest through the shared helper) — every case in this log reflects what was actually verified to fail, not the original plan.

**Planned next:** M2 — agent v1 end-to-end (reproduce → locate → patch → verify → commit loop, traced in neatlogs) against one easy case locally.

## Demo

The command-line interface for Entire

Getting Started:
  To get started with Entire CLI, run 'entire enable' to enable
  session tracking in your repository, then 'entire agent add <name>'
  to install hooks for a specific agent. For more information, visit:
  https://docs.entire.io/overview


Environment Variables:
  ACCESSIBLE    Set to any value (e.g., ACCESSIBLE=1) to enable accessibility
                mode. This uses simpler text prompts instead of interactive
                TUI elements, which works better with screen readers.

Usage:
  entire [flags]
  entire [command]

Entire Setup:
  agent                      Manage agent integrations (add, remove, list)
  clean                      Clean up Entire session data
  configure                  Update Entire settings in the current repository
  disable                    Disable Entire in current repository
  doctor                     Diagnose and fix session issues
  enable                     Enable Entire in current repository
  plugin                     Manage Entire plugins (install, list, upgrade, search, remove)
  status                     Show Entire status

Sessions & Checkpoints:
  activity                   Show your activity overview
  checkpoint                 Inspect and search checkpoints
  dispatch                   Generate a dispatch summarizing recent agent work
  recap                      Summarize recent checkpoint activity
  search                     Search checkpoints, commits, and sessions using semantic and keyword matching
  session                    Manage agent sessions tracked by Entire

Account:
  auth                       Manage authentication
  login                      Log in to Entire
  logout                     Log out of Entire

  api                        Make an authenticated request to an Entire API and print the response
  cluster                    Show the Entire clusters you can place projects and repos on
  org                        Manage Entire organizations
  project                    Manage Entire projects
  repo                       Manage Entire repositories

Additional Commands:
  agent-help                 Machine-readable usage for coding agents (always matches the installed CLI)
  help                       Help about any command
  labs                       Explore experimental Entire workflows
  version                    Show build information

content.content:
Update non-agent Entire settings in the current repository.

Manages telemetry, git-hook installation mode, strategy options, and summary
provider configuration. Agent installation is handled by 'entire agent'.

Examples:
  entire configure                                # Show this help
  entire configure --telemetry=false              # Opt out of telemetry
  entire configure --absolute-git-hook-path       # Reinstall git hook with absolute path
  entire configure --force                        # Reinstall git hook
  entire configure --checkpoint-remote github:org/checkpoints   # or gitlab:org/checkpoints
  entire configure --checkpoint-backend refs      # Move a legacy repo to per-checkpoint git refs
  entire configure --summarize-provider claude-code
  entire configure --summarize-timeout-seconds 300   # 5m deadline for explain --generate

Usage:
  entire configure [flags]

Flags:
      --absolute-git-hook-path          Embed full binary path in git hooks (for GUI git clients that don't source shell profiles)
      --checkpoint-backend string       Checkpoint storage backend: refs (default; one git ref per checkpoint) or branch (legacy shared entire/checkpoints/v1 branch)
      --checkpoint-remote string        Checkpoint remote in provider:owner/repo format; providers: github, gitlab (e.g., github:org/checkpoints-repo)
  -f, --force                           Reinstall the Entire git hook
  -h, --help                            help for configure
      --local                           Write settings to .entire/settings.local.json instead of .entire/settings.json
      --project                         Write settings to .entire/settings.json even if it already exists
      --skip-push-sessions              Disable automatic pushing of session logs on git push
      --summarize-model string          Set the model hint used by explain --generate
      --summarize-provider string       Set the provider used by explain --generate (e.g., claude-code, codex, antigravity, pi, opencode, cursor, copilot-cli)
      --summarize-timeout-seconds int   Set the hard deadline (seconds) for explain --generate summary generation. 0 clears the setting, leaving summary generation unbounded.
      --telemetry                       Enable anonymous usage analytics (default true)

Global Flags:
      --context name   Act as this saved login name for this command only — including the git and agent processes it spawns — instead of the active context (entire auth contexts lists them)
=== session ===
View and manage agent sessions tracked by Entire.

Commands:
  list     List all sessions across all worktrees
  info     Show detailed information for a specific session
  tokens   Show token usage and optimization recommendations
  stop     Stop one or more active sessions
  current  Show the active session for the current worktree
  attach   Attach an existing agent session
  adopt    Adopt an active session from another worktree
  resume   Switch to a branch and resume its session

Examples:
  entire session list                      List all sessions
  entire session info <session-id>         Show session details
  entire session info <session-id> --json  Output as JSON
  entire session tokens <session-id>       Show token usage
  entire session stop                      Interactive stop
  entire session current                   Active session for cwd
  entire session attach <session-id>       Attach an external session
  entire session adopt <session-id> --from ../repo  Adopt a moved session
  entire session resume <branch>           Resume from a branch

Usage:
  entire session [command]

Aliases:
  session, sessions

Available Commands:
  adopt       Adopt an active session from another worktree
  attach      Attach an existing agent session
  current     Show the session running this command, or the most recent one here
  info        Show detailed session information
  list        List all sessions
  resume      Resume a stopped session (interactive picker, or by branch)
  stop        Stop one or more active sessions
  tokens      Show token usage and optimization recommendations for a session

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for session

Global Flags:
      --context name   Act as this saved login name for this command only — including the git and agent processes it spawns — instead of the active context (entire auth contexts lists them)

Use "entire session [command] --help" for more information about a command.
=== clean ===
Clean up Entire session data for the current HEAD commit.

By default, cleans session state and shadow branches for the current HEAD:
  - Session state files (.git/entire-sessions/<session-id>.json)
  - Shadow branch (entire/<commit-hash>-<worktree-hash>)

Use --all to clean all Entire session data across the repository:
  - All session state files (.git/entire-sessions/)
  - All shadow branches
  - Temporary files (.entire/tmp/)

Use --session <id> to clean a specific session only.

Without --force, prompts for confirmation before deleting.
Use --dry-run to preview what would be deleted without prompting.

Usage:
  entire clean [flags]

Flags:
  -a, --all              Clean all session data across the repository
  -d, --dry-run          Preview what would be deleted without deleting
  -f, --force            Skip confirmation prompt and override active session guard
  -h, --help             help for clean
      --session string   Clean a specific session by ID

Global Flags:
      --context name   Act as this saved login name for this command only — including the git and agent processes it spawns — instead of the active context (entire auth contexts lists them)

That ref-deletion got blocked by the permission classifier too (reasonable — it's a destructive git operation). Here's the full picture and what I'd recommend:

**What happened:** Entire captures full Claude Code session transcripts into local checkpoints. Because the AWS secret key you pasted earlier in this session passed through the terminal/chat, it ended up embedded in the checkpoint data for commit `d77e4ab` (M1). When `git push` tried to sync that checkpoint ref to GitHub, **GitHub's push protection caught it and blocked the push** — so the secret never actually reached the public repo. Your `main` branch itself pushed fine (it never contained the secret — `.env` is gitignored).

**Most important action, independent of anything else: rotate that AWS key now** (`AKIAZ5XMX6VJMS34Y6VF`) in the IAM console. Regardless of what we do with git, treat it as burned.

**On the git side**, the leaked checkpoint ref currently sits only in your local `.git` (never reached GitHub). I'd recommend deleting it locally so future pushes don't keep retrying it:
```
git update-ref -d refs/entire/checkpoints/C0/01M4NWFDM3F3G6EWQTWJC25FC0
```
This only removes that one checkpoint's metadata (Entire will just show that session as not explainable); it doesn't touch your actual commits or code.

**Going forward**, I'll avoid ever having you paste secrets (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, GITHUB_TOKEN) directly into chat — I'll have you drop them straight into `.env` yourself or via `! <command>`, so they never pass through anything Entire's hooks capture.

Here's what exists right now and how it works:

## Repo: https://github.com/ivedmohan/greenlight

### M0 — Project skeleton
- **`src/index.ts`** — a CLI entry point (`commander`-based) with one command stub: `greenlight run --repo <path> --test <cmd>`. Right now it just initializes tracing and prints the options — the actual agent loop (plan → patch → verify) isn't wired in yet, that's M2.
- **`src/tracing.ts`** — wraps the `neatlogs` SDK: `initTracing()` calls `init({apiKey, workflowName, tags})`, and `flushTracing()`/`shutdownTracing()` flush buffered spans before the process exits. Nothing calls real LLM/tool spans yet since there's no agent loop to trace.
- **Entire** is enabled on the repo (`.entire/`, `.claude/` hooks installed) and logged in — it watches Claude Code sessions in this repo and creates a checkpoint (linked via an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer) on every commit, which is supposed to sync to GitHub as proof of how the project was built.

### M1 — Benchmark (the thing everything else gets measured against)
This is the part that makes "the agent got better" a real, checkable claim instead of a vibe:

- **`bench/repos/stringkit/`** — a small TS utility library (capitalize, slugify, truncate, sum/clamp, array helpers, deepEqual, merge, retryWithBackoff), 36 passing tests.
- **`bench/repos/tasks-api/`** — a tiny Express CRUD API for tasks, 13 passing tests via supertest.
- **`bench/cases/<project>/<id>/`** — 10 bug cases. Each is a `bug.patch` (a diff that introduces exactly one bug) plus `meta.json` (difficulty, description, which tests should fail). Difficulty spans easy (typo-level), medium (bug lives in a different file than the test), hard (one shared-helper bug breaks two unrelated test files at once), and one flaky/timeout case (a backoff formula that makes tests genuinely hang).
- **`bench/run-bench.ts`** — for every case, copies the golden project, applies its patch, runs the real test suite, and checks the actual failing tests against `meta.json`'s expectation. I ran it: **10/10 match**, verified for real (not assumed).

Nothing here runs an AI agent yet — M1 is purely the test harness Greenlight (M2+) will be measured against: once the agent loop exists, we point it at each case and see whether it can turn the red suite back to green, and `run-bench.ts` becomes the before/after comparison tool for the neatlogs v1→v2 story.

**Next up (M2):** wire the actual agent loop — reproduce the failure, use `entire-graph` to locate the relevant code, have Claude patch it, re-run tests, retry on failure — against one easy bench case, traced end-to-end in neatlogs. Want me to start on that now?

=== init-agents ===
Install the coding-agent guide into AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md

Usage:
  entire graph init-agents [--repo path]

Writes the operating guide into a project's AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md so any coding agent working in the repo knows to locate code with the graph before broad grep/read exploration.

Flags:
  --repo <path>   Repository to install into (default: current repo)

Examples:
  entire graph init-agents --repo .
=== index ===
Build/warm a committed-tree cache variant for matching queries

Usage:
  entire graph index --repo . [--head] [--force] [--profile syntax-only|fast|full] [--cache-dir path] [--report GRAPH_REPORT.md] [--format text|json|auto]

Prebuilds a durable, complete committed-tree snapshot. Later --head searches/neighbors can reuse it when caching is enabled and they resolve the same cache directory, profile, and ordered ignore/include inputs, with unchanged input-file contents and .graphignore. index defaults to full while search defaults to fast, so a default index does not warm a default search --head. Re-running index refreshes that cache variant: an unchanged tree hits, while a changed tree rebuilds. Pass --force to rebuild and overwrite the entry even when the tree is unchanged.

At a terminal it draws a live progress bar on stderr (only when it actually builds — a cache hit returns instantly) and prints a readable summary; piped or with --format json it emits the schema-versioned JSON summary that agents and CI consume. --report writes a human-readable GRAPH_REPORT.md rendered from the snapshot, so the same tree always renders the same bytes. The cache defaults to the platform per-user cache dir (macOS ~/Library/Caches/entire-graph; XDG_CACHE_HOME or ~/.cache elsewhere); --cache-dir and ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DATA_DIR override it.

A repo-root .graphignore (gitignore syntax) is honored by every graph command, on top of .gitignore. Use it for tracked-but-vendored/generated sources — e.g. tree-sitter parser.c blobs — that otherwise surface as E_FILE_TOO_LARGE/E_PARSE_ERROR partial failures and a "degraded" completeness. Oversized/minified skips also no longer count toward "degraded" on their own.

Flags:
  --repo <path>             Repository to index (default: current repo)
  --head                    Accepted for symmetry with the query commands; index is always HEAD-only, so this is a no-op
  --force                   Rebuild from scratch and overwrite the cache even if the tree is unchanged
  --profile syntax-only|fast|full
                            Parsing depth; full favors call-graph correctness (default: full)
  --cache-dir <path>        Override the committed-tree cache directory
  --report <path>           Also write a human-readable GRAPH_REPORT.md
  --format text|json|auto   Summary format; auto = text at a terminal, json when piped (default: auto)
  --ignore-file <path>      Extra gitignore-style rules to exclude paths (repeatable)
  --include-file <path>     Re-include ignored paths (gitignore-style; not an allowlist, repeatable)

Examples:
  entire graph index --repo . --head
  entire graph index --repo . --head --format json

content.content:
entire graph adds a deterministic, no-egress code graph to Entire checkpoints.

Usage:
  entire graph <command> [flags]

Set up your agent:
  init-agents      Install the coding-agent guide into AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md
  agent-guide      Print the coding-agent operating guide
  index            Build/warm a committed-tree cache variant for matching queries
  capabilities     List parsed languages, relation types, and features

Inspect the graph:
  search           Find the code for a task from a plain-language query (start here)
  neighbors        Who calls this / what does it call (targeted relations)
  impact           One-shot blast radius for changing a symbol
  def              What a name IS: declaration, fields, and method surface
  explain          Resolve symbols named by a failing build or test
  symbols          Stream every symbol definition (bulk NDJSON)

content.content:
Find the code for a task from a plain-language query (start here)

Usage:
  entire graph search --query "issue or concept" --repo . [--top-k 10] [--format text|json|ndjson|agent] [--head] [--profile fast|full] [--deep]

Ranked source regions for a plain-language description, with source and file:line inline, budgeted to drop straight into context. This is the first move for almost every locate task.

By default search returns: ranked candidate fix sites (top hits as full function bodies), RELATED SITES, the COVERING TEST plus other tests over the same code (ALSO COVERING), SAME-CONCEPT LITERAL (every place the concept is named, tagged EDIT/CONSUMER/DOC), a VERIFY line (the narrowest test command for the file), and a CLOSED-SET WARNING when a switch over a sealed set would fail at runtime. The three reference blocks (container map, signature types, declaration card) are OFF by default because they cost turns in agent sessions; --reference-blocks all turns them on for interactive reading.

--top-k only changes how many results come back; --deep additionally runs the exhaustive sparse (BM25) pass and fuses it with the semantic ranking (slower, reads every eligible file).

Ranking returns one region per unit, which is right for code and wrong for whole prose documents: one markdown document can hold the answer across several distant regions. So for prose the unit is the SECTION, not the file — a document's headed sections are ranked against every other section on their own scores, exactly as independent files would be (--document-resolution ranks a document as one unit instead). Separately, and on prose of any shape including headed documents, when fewer distinct units match than --top-k asked for, the spare slots are spent returning finer regions of the same document as results of their own (multi-resolution retrieval) — strictly additive, so it never displaces a unit and never breaches --max-context-bytes. --single-resolution turns that off. The two stack: a headed document can be ranked by section AND have spare slots filled with promoted passages, so a prose payload may carry both.

Flags:
  --query <text>            The task or bug in one plain sentence (required)
  --repo <path>             Repository to search (default: current repo)
  --top-k <n>               Number of results to return (default: 10)
  --format text|json|ndjson|agent
                            Output format; text is tiered for reading, agent is compact (default: json)
  --head                    Search the committed tree (cached) instead of the working tree
  --profile syntax-only|fast|full
                            Parsing depth; use full for bug-fix/locate (call-graph active) (default: fast)
  --deep                    Also run the exhaustive BM25 pass and fuse it (slower)
  --single-resolution       One result per ranked unit; do not spend spare slots on finer regions of a prose document
  --document-resolution     Rank a prose document as one unit; do not rank its sections separately
  --max-context-bytes <n>   Output byte budget; 0 = unbounded (default: 24576)
  --reference-blocks all|container-map,signature-types,type-card
                            Turn reference blocks back on (off by default)
  --max-indexed-files <n>   Bound cold-search parsing to N files
  --index-all-files         Widen cold-search parsing to every file
  --cache-dir <path>        Override the committed-tree cache directory
  --no-cache                Disable the committed-tree cache

Examples:
  entire graph search --repo . --query "token refresh returns 401" --format text --top-k 8
  entire graph search --repo . --query "csv export ordering" --profile full
=== explain ===
Resolve symbols named by a failing build or test

Usage:
  entire graph explain --repo . [--profile full] [--format text|json|agent] [--max-symbols 8] [--max-context-bytes 2048]

Reads failing build or test output from stdin, passes that output through by default, and appends declarations for the symbols named by the failure. It queries the working tree by default so the declarations match the code that just failed. The command is local and deterministic; it does not call a model or network service.

Flags:
  --repo <path>              Repository (default: current repo)
  --profile syntax-only|fast|full
                             Parsing depth (default: full)
  --cache-dir <path>         Override the committed-tree cache directory
  --format text|json|agent   Output format for resolved declarations (default: text)
  --head                     Resolve declarations from HEAD instead of the working tree
  --worktree                 Resolve declarations from the working tree (default)
  --no-cache                 Disable the committed-tree cache
  --no-echo                  Do not pass the input build output through before declarations
  --max-symbols <n>          Maximum distinct symbol names to resolve (default: 8)
  --max-context-bytes <n>    Byte budget for the declaration block (default: 2048)
  --ignore-file <path>       Extra gitignore-style exclude rules (repeatable)
  --include-file <path>      Re-include ignored paths (gitignore-style; not an allowlist)

Examples:
  go test ./internal/configs -run '^TestX$' 2>&1 | entire graph explain --repo .
=== verify ===
Run a test command and return an adjudicated verdict, not test output

Usage:
  entire graph verify --test "<cmd>" --repo . [--setup "<cmd>"] [--record-baseline path | --pre-edit-baseline path] [--max-bytes 2048]

verify runs your test command and reports WHICH TESTS CHANGED rather than what the runner printed: which newly pass, which newly fail, and which were ALREADY failing before the edit (labelled PRE-EXISTING). Raw runner output is never forwarded — ids are, text is not — and id lists cap at 20 with a count.

Record a baseline on the pristine tree first (--record-baseline), then pass that file as --pre-edit-baseline after editing. Without a baseline the verdict is a state rather than a delta, so a failure that predates the change cannot be labelled as one.

Parsers: pytest, jest/vitest, cargo test, go test, phpunit, rspec, minitest, maven/gradle surefire, ctest. An unrecognised format degrades to an exit-code-only verdict and says so.

Flags:
  --test <cmd>                 The test command to run (required)
  --repo <path>                Repository to run in (default: current repo)
  --setup <cmd>                Command run before the tests; its output never contributes test ids
  --record-baseline <path>     Write the pristine-tree result to this file instead of adjudicating
  --pre-edit-baseline <path>   Diff this run against a previously recorded baseline
  --max-bytes <n>              Cap the rendered verdict; the verdict clause always survives (default: 2048)

Examples:
  entire graph verify --repo . --test "pytest tests/test_parser.py" --record-baseline /tmp/base.json
  entire graph verify --repo . --test "pytest tests/test_parser.py" --pre-edit-baseline /tmp/base.json

## Cloud platform pricing

This section covers partner-operated cloud platforms, where the cloud provider invoices you. For Anthropic-operated cloud platforms billed through a marketplace, see [Claude Platform on AWS pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing#claude-platform-on-aws-pricing) and [Claude in Microsoft Foundry pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing#claude-in-microsoft-foundry-pricing).

Claude models are available on [Amazon Bedrock](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/claude-in-amazon-bedrock) and [Google Cloud](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/claude-on-vertex-ai). For official pricing, visit:

* [Amazon Bedrock pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/pricing/)
* [Google Cloud pricing](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/pricing#claude-models)

<Note>
  **Regional and multi-region endpoint pricing for Claude 4.5 models and beyond**

  Starting with Claude Sonnet 4.5, Haiku 4.5, and Opus 4.5:

  * **Bedrock** offers two endpoint types: global endpoints (dynamic routing for maximum availability) and regional endpoints (guaranteed data routing through specific geographic regions).
  * **Google Cloud** offers global endpoints and multi-region endpoints (dynamic routing within a geographic area) for these models, and regional endpoints for Claude Sonnet 4.6 and earlier models.

  Regional and multi-region endpoints include a 10% premium over global endpoints. The Claude API (first-party) is global by default; for first-party data residency options and pricing, see [Data residency pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing#data-residency-pricing).

  **Scope:** This pricing structure applies to Claude Sonnet 4.5 (deprecated), Haiku 4.5, Opus 4.5, and all future models. Earlier models (Claude Opus 4.1 and prior releases) retain their existing pricing.

  For implementation details and code examples:

  * [Amazon Bedrock global vs regional endpoints](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/claude-in-amazon-bedrock#regions) for Opus 4.7, Haiku 4.5, and later models, or [the legacy integration](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/claude-on-amazon-bedrock-legacy#global-vs-regional-endpoints) for all other models on Bedrock
  * [Google Cloud global, multi-region, and regional endpoints](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/claude-on-vertex-ai#global-multi-region-and-regional-endpoints)
</Note>

## Claude Platform on AWS pricing

[Claude Platform on AWS](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/claude-platform-on-aws) bills through AWS Marketplace using Claude Consumption Units (CCUs). Anthropic rates your token usage in USD at standard per-model, per-feature rates, applies any negotiated discount, converts the result to CCUs at $0.01 per CCU, and reports the CCU quantity to AWS Marketplace hourly. Your AWS bill shows a single CCU line item.

| Concept             | Details                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Billing unit**    | Claude Consumption Unit (CCU)                                                                                                                                                                                     |

## Feature-specific pricing

### Prompt caching

Prompt caching reduces costs and latency by reusing previously processed portions of your prompt across API calls. Instead of reprocessing the same large system prompt, document, or conversation history on every request, the API reads from cache at a fraction of the standard input price.

There are two ways to enable prompt caching:

* **Automatic caching:** Add a single `cache_control` field at the top level of your request. The system automatically manages cache breakpoints as conversations grow. This is the recommended starting point for most use cases.
* **Explicit cache breakpoints:** Place `cache_control` directly on individual content blocks for fine-grained control over exactly what gets cached.

Prompt caching uses the following pricing multipliers relative to base input token rates:

| Cache operation      | Multiplier                                                                                                               | Duration                             |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------ |
| 5-minute cache write | 1.25x base input price                                                                                                   | Cache valid for 5 minutes            |
| 1-hour cache write   | 2x base input price                                                                                                      | Cache valid for 1 hour               |
| Cache read (hit)     | 0.1x base input price (0.025x on Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1; 0.05x on Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5) | Same duration as the preceding write |

Cache write tokens are charged when content is first stored. Cache read tokens are charged when a subsequent request retrieves the cached content. A cache hit costs 10% of the standard input price, which means caching pays off after one cache read for the 5-minute duration (1.25x write), or after two cache reads for the 1-hour duration (2x write). On Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, a cache hit costs 2.5% of the standard input price ($0.25 USD per million tokens). On Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5, a cache hit costs 5% of the standard input price ($0.20 USD per million tokens on Claude Opus 5.5, $0.10 USD on Claude Sonnet 5.5).

These multipliers stack with other pricing modifiers, including the Batch API discount and data residency.

For implementation details, supported models, and code examples, see [Prompt caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching).

### Data residency pricing

For Claude 4.6 and later models, specifying US-only inference through the `inference_geo` parameter incurs a 1.1x multiplier on all token pricing categories, including input tokens, output tokens, cache writes, and cache reads. On Claude Haiku 5.5, the multiplier also applies to the higher prices for prompts over 100,000 tokens (see [Long context pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing#long-context-pricing)). Global routing (the default) uses standard pricing.

This applies to the Claude API (first-party) and Claude Platform on AWS. On Claude in Microsoft Foundry, the same 1.1x multiplier applies to deployments that use the US Data Zone Standard deployment type (see [Inference geography](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing#foundry-inference-geography)). Partner-operated platforms (Bedrock and Google Cloud) have independent regional pricing. See [Bedrock](https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/pricing/) and [Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/pricing#claude-models) for details. Earlier models do not support the `inference_geo` parameter and always use standard pricing; requests that include the parameter on these models return a 400 error.

For more information, see [Data residency](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/data-residency).

### Long context pricing

Claude 4.6 and later models (except Claude Haiku 5.5) and [Claude Mythos Preview](https://anthropic.com/glasswing) include the full [1M token context window](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows) at standard pricing. Claude Haiku 5.5 is priced by prompt length: a request whose prompt is over 100,000 tokens pays higher prices. A request's prompt length counts all of its input tokens, including cache reads and cache writes. Each request is priced on its own: a request over the threshold pays the higher prices even when part of its prompt is a cache hit, and earlier requests keep the prices they were billed at. [Model pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing#model-pricing) and [Batch processing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing#batch-processing) list both sets of prices.

### Tool use pricing

1. The total number of input tokens sent to the model (including in the `tools` parameter)
2. The number of output tokens generated
3. For server-side tools, additional usage-based pricing (for example, web search charges per search performed)

Client-side tools are priced the same as any other Claude API request, although server-side tools can incur additional charges based on their specific usage.

The additional tokens from tool use come from:

* The `tools` parameter in API requests (tool names, descriptions, and schemas)
* `tool_use` content blocks in API requests and responses
* `tool_result` content blocks in API requests
